en: I. Folio 1:

Bower Manuscript, Part 1 Oṃ! [There was] a mountain whose peaks were inhabited by hosts of gods, ṛṣis, siddhas, kinnaras, nāgas, yakṣas, and vidyādharas; it possessed infinite jewels and was as meritorious as the delightful celestial realm of Tripiṣṭapa, exalted and sublime. (1) Upon it, during the nights of the rainy season, the waters were agitated by the mass of rays from thousands of shimmering gems, which seemed to flee in fear in the ten directions, making one suspect that the moon, stars, sun, and fire had all taken up residence there. (2)

Moreover, darkness does not approach it. It is that place which is constantly served by numerous hosts of sages together with their disciples, who carry in their hands sacrificial wood, *kuśa* grass, fruits, water, and flowers; and whose trees in the groves have their branches rubbed by the celestial nymphs seeking blossoms. There, because of the constant contact with the rays of the moon resting upon a portion of the matted locks and crown of the Three-eyed Lord, the water is cool even by day, appearing like Himalayan crystal stone.

5. From which [mountain] moonstones flow abundantly; whose delightful groves, their rocky surfaces washed by waters released from the clouds and resounding with the songs of various flocks of birds, are densely filled with trees bearing flowers and fruit;

and where, at night, medicinal herbs blaze like fire. 6. With lions who bear a mass of manes whiter than the rays of the moon, who scatter particles of blood from the temples of rutting elephants, and who let out loud roars from the mouths of mountain caves—

Even the roar of a multitude of clouds is not tolerated where [the silence prevails]. On that mountain—which is the ornament of the circle of the earth, which acts like a universal guest by bestowing its wealth upon the world, and whose peaks are beautiful with trees bearing flowers and fruits in all seasons—these sages, whose darkness has been dispelled, dwell. Ātreya, Hārīta, Parāśara, Bhela, Garga, Śāmbavya, Suśruta, Vasiṣṭha, Karāla, and Kāpya reside there, desiring to know the names, qualities, forms, and potencies of all medicinal herbs.

9. Gathering by the hundreds, they moved forward. Having seen [the tree] with leaves that were a vibrant green, shining like sapphire, and with bulbs as white as jasmine, crystal, the moon, moonbeams, conch shells, clouds, and snow; Suśruta, having conceived a desire for [the medicine], approached the Sage, the King of Kāśī, asking, "What might this be? Then the Blessed One spoke to him as it truly was: 9. "In ancient times, when the nectar (*amṛta*) was churned, the Lord of Asuras drank from it himself. The Blessed One then severed his head."
10. Janārdana. 11. When his head was severed, the throat-vein was close at hand; drops fell upon the earth—this indeed was his first birth here.

I. Fol. 2: Bower Manuscript, r1 The Brahmins do not eat it because it has emerged from contact with the body; for this very reason, those proficient in the mastery of the scriptures declare its pungent odor. (12) Because it is devoid of the salty taste (*lavaṇa-rasa*), they call it *raśūna*;

however, its well-known designation in common usage is *laśuna*. What is the use of many local dialect names mentioned here? Listen rather to its taste, quality, and potency, and [the results] from its medicinal application. (13) It is declared to be pungent (*kaṭu*) both in its primary taste (*rasa*) and in its post-digestive transformation (*pāka*).

Likewise, another variety is described as sweet when cooked; it is light in odor, difficult to digest in its potency (*vīrya*), and renowned for being heating and aphrodisiac. Because of its sourness, heat, and oily nature, it is declared by the bulls among sages to diminish the strength of *vāta*. Due to its sweetness and its pitta-like quality, as well as its flavor, it pacifies *pitta*. Because of its heating, sharp, and pungent qualities, it is proclaimed by the wise to conquer the strength of *kapha* and destroy all diseases.

When prepared according to the prescribed method, it removes the three *doṣas*. It destroys wind (*vāta*) even when it has reached the bones, and it quickly pacifies phlegm (*kapha*), even when recently arisen. It generates a powerful digestive fire (*agni-bala*) and is considered the most excellent for bestowing strength and complexion.

Now, indeed, this festival of garlic should be employed here by those who consume various kinds of wine, meat, and ghee, and who eat barley and wheat—those who are constitutionally inclined toward comfort—during the months of Nabhah, Madhu, and Mādhava.

7–8. In that season, girdles suitable for chariots are cast aside by amorous women; pearl necklaces are removed from their chests because they cause pain from the pressure of the breasts due to the cold. The enjoyment of palace rooftops, though beautiful with the intermingling of moonbeams, is no longer desired. At that time, agallochum (agaru) is highly esteemed, as are saffron marks and musk. Furthermore, one should arrange on the ground at the tops of palaces, at gateways, and at the doors of upper chambers garlands of garlic rich in bulbs.

In the same way, one should offer worship; one should place garlands made of that [substance] upon the attendant and the people. This is the rule prescribed for the people, known by its very small measure. Then, having purified his body, being clean and secluded, and having honored the gods, the Brahmins, and the fire, he should drink the fresh juice of garlic—filtered through the edge of a cloth—on a day joined with an auspicious planet and asterism. He should drink a *kuḍava*, or half a *kuḍava*, or a *kuḍava* and a half, or even more than that.

Indeed, no fixed measure [of wine] is prescribed here; one should observe the humors (*doṣa*), strength, and diseases before drinking. While he drinks, one should gently sprinkle him with the auspicious breezes from fans made of palm leaves.

If, however, fainting occurs while he is drinking, one should then touch him with cold water mixed with sandalwood. One who has fainted from the third part of the liquor should drink a single mouthful of meat-broth, first for the purpose of performing the "play of the throat" (*galakrīḍi*).

Having remained thus for a moment, he should drink [the medicine] while leaving some remainder. (23) When that has been digested, he should eat milk-rice or boiled *śāli* rice; he should be nourished with milk, or with the meat-broths of wild animals (*jāṅgala*), or with heart-pleasing soups prepared with pulses (*vaidala*), combined with fats in the proper measure at one time. (24) He should drink *mārdvīka* wine, or honey, or *madhūka* wine, or *śāta-madirā*, or *ariṣṭa*, or *śīdhu*, or *jagala*, or *agaja*, or *maireya*; or whatever other medicinal liquor there may be, he should drink it mixed with water, or each one separately.

It becomes like an intoxicating mixture. (25) One who does not drink liquor may drink pleasant water, as well as sour *kāñjika*; one may also drink *tuṣodaka*, *suvīraja*, and pure *mastu*. (26) One should never eat this with molasses, nor should one drink it with raw water.

6. One should consume it regularly, always being wary of indigestion, and should not eat it for many days. Then, having ground smooth and auspicious tubers and mixing them with an equal amount of ghee, one should churn this together with a churning-stick in a vessel of clarified butter. 28.

7. From the tenth day onwards, one should consume [the medicine] in a dose equal to a *bilva* fruit when it has been digested; and once it is digested, one should follow the dietary rules prescribed in the *Rasakalpa*. 8. These two pre-eminent methods have both been declared by me; one should be diligent in these two. Listen now to other methods from me. [One should eat] bulbs that have the luster of conch shells and are free of impurities, along with parched grain flour (*saktu*), half-cooked barley (*kulmāsa*), and *cukra*, combined with preparations of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and oil, various kinds of soups and meats, and powdered mung beans mixed with *harītaka*.

One should eat other [medicinal] substances prepared with many other refinements enriched by *gandhasauvarcala* salt (v. 32). Having prepared its stalk together with meats, one should give him that strained, pure, and heart-pleasing broth to drink; likewise, one should give him milk that has been processed in this way, or a pulse-based soup (*yūṣa*) mixed with that same preparation (v. 32). Furthermore, having coated garlic together with oil and vinegar in a vessel placed among barley grains and sealed with clay, a man who consumes it after it has remained there for one year will [overcome] those [afflictions] that have persisted for a very long time.
11. ...he even abandons diseases. // 33 // When a cow that has resided in the Three Jewels (*triratna*) becomes devoid of grass, then one should provide half a portion of grass [and] garlic.
I. Fol. 3:

Bower Manuscript r1 Milk, curd, clarified butter, or even buttermilk—a Brahmin, having employed these, shall overcome various diseases and attain well-being. // 34 // Thirty-two *prasthas* of garlic juice...

2. Half a half-measure of fermenting agent (*kiṇva*) from this [mixture], one *prastha* of oil free from impurities, and six measures of flour should be added. One should also add a jar of the decoction of *meṣaśṛṅgī*. 3. When it has become well-cooled, the wise man should again pour two *prasthas* of flour into it. Thus, after five days, this excellent wine (*sureya*) becomes endowed with the qualities of juice, color, and fragrance; this oil, so highly praised, is known as the "Exceedingly Potent" (*atyarthakārmuka*). The person who diligently employs this oil, or even this wine, [shall obtain great results].

The hosts of diseases avoid him in battle, as if they were others facing those skilled in weaponry. Having ground one *prastha* of purified garlic and mixed it with powders of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and half a *palita* measure, along with one *kuḍava* each of ghee and oil, this preparation, when administered for ten days, is said to destroy cough, dyspnea, and indigestion. When combined with wind-alleviating drugs, it destroys *māruta-gulma*.

When combined with *khadira*, it destroys leprosy (*kuṣṭa*) as soon as it is applied. When mixed with *hayagandhā*, it cures cough and asthma; when mixed with *madhuyaṣṭī*, it is said to be beneficial for the voice. This [preparation], when joined with various specific substances, destroys manifold diseases. There is no restriction whatsoever in this ritual procedure (*kalpa*); however this *kalpa* is employed by those seeking well-being, it is the best among elixirs (*rasāyana*).

Listen with a focused mind, O Suśruta, as I describe briefly its nine qualities: it dispels leprosy, anorexia, abdominal tumors, cough, emaciation, vitiligo, and loss of digestive fire; it removes wind-disorders, menorrhagia, colic, consumption, abdominal enlargement, splenic disorders, and hemorrhoids; it cures hemiplegia, stiffness of the waist, worms, diseases, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and urinary disorders; and it destroys drowsiness, chronic rhinitis, weakness of the arms, back-wind, and epilepsy. It is glorious, possessing the beautiful resonance of a flute or drum, the luster of refined gold at its tip, and it bestows intelligence, memory, and strength.

11. A man whose body is well-knit, who is free from wrinkles and other signs of decay, and who possesses all his senses firm and ever-increasingly vigorous, with a steady digestive fire and strength, shall live for a hundred years, or remain undecaying among women.

42. This ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for garlic has been declared by me, and it was likewise observed by the ancient sages. Let one who applies it correctly [attain] such [results] as have been described. 43. [The verse continues: ... [as seen] by the former sages, let him employ it properly... [the rest of the verse follows].

The equilibrium of the elements that digest food is indeed health; likewise, nourishment, vitality, energy, and even longevity arise from the digestive fire (*agni*). For fire is the root of food, and the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) have digestion as their root. From the equilibrium of the constituents comes health, and from health comes nourishment.

3. This is the best [type of fire]. // 45 // Through nourishment, vitality, as well as enthusiasm, and by all these, the life of living beings increases; therefore, one should first examine the fire. // 46 // That which is balanced due to the equilibrium of the elements is called "equal" (sama); it is indeed proclaimed to be the most excellent. In the case of imbalance, one should drink ghee mixed with curd or the *havuṣādi* [decoction]. // 47 //

48–49. When the digestive fire (*agni*) is weak, unctuous and warm suppositories are desired, as are unctuous drinks and foods. However, when it is sluggish, fasting (*laṅghana*) should come first, followed by digestive (*pācana*) and appetizing (*dīpana*) treatments. The administration of powders (*cūrṇa*) and fermented liquors (*ariṣṭa*) that alleviate *pitta* and *kapha* is also beneficial. Physicians should apply these measures according to what is suitable for the patient when the fire is balanced. 50. There is a verse on this point: "When the fire is sluggish or too sharp, a person dies even without [severe] complications; when it is irregular, there is an abundance of diseases; but when it is balanced, one lives long and happily. Therefore, in all diseases and at all times, the wise physician should know that treatment has its root in the digestive fire."

It should be prepared afterwards for the pacification of disease. (51) One who desires intelligence, health, and strength, and who wishes to live long, should employ *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *brāhmī*, *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, and *madhuka* with their own juices. (52) By [using this] for one month, one becomes intelligent; after six months, one becomes a retainer of what has been heard (*śrutadhara*) and free from old age. By practicing this properly for two years, one lives for a thousand years. (53) Thus, by employing it further and further, one becomes free from old age. — — — — // {O} [The remainder of the line is blank]

In gruels, meat soups, and vegetable broths; in electuaries, powders, and medicinal formulations; in pills, collyria, suppositories, and in the administration of smoke and insufflations (pradhamana); and in the procedures of puṭapāka, tarpaṇa, sudation, emesis, and eye-drops (āścyotana). // 55–56 //

57–58. Furthermore, regarding other [substances] not mentioned, where no portion has been specified, there should be an equal portion of the ingredients; however, honey and clarified butter should be double [the quantity]. One should add three parts of treacle and four parts of powdered sugar. Where no liquid is indicated among the substances to be ground, water is intended there. 59. In the case of curd, urine, milk, clarified butter, hair, horns, and hooves, one should provide everything from a cow (*gavya*). Among honeys, that produced by *mākṣika* bees is to be used. [Likewise for] pomegranate bark...

One should cook it together with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*). By this, both ears, the female organ, the lips, and the penis—all these—will grow. (60) Half a *phala* of *citraka*, as well as one *karṣa* each of the roots of *tṛvṛt* and *sātalā*;
(61) [one *karṣa*] each of the roots of the elephant (*dantin*), of *pippalī*, of rock salt (*saindhava*), of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), of sour cane (*amlavetasa*), and twenty of the excellent *abhayā*.
(Folio 4, Bower Manuscript)

One should properly prepare ten *modaka* pills from eight *palas* of treacle. One should eat one of them every tenth day for the purpose of ripening the bodily humors (*doṣas*). Thereafter, one should drink warm water following the dose to facilitate digestion. At the conclusion of the purgation, one should bathe and then consume suitable food. In this matter, there is no restriction whatsoever regarding speech, body, or mind at any time; this purgative, devised by Agasti, is suitable for all seasons for kings. It destroys old age and death, eradicates all diseases, is aphrodisiac, and acts as a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).

66–67. This [treatment] increases intelligence and health. It must never be given to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, under any circumstances. It should not be given to those hostile to the king, nor to others who are evildoers. 68. Two *pañcamūlas*, *madhuka*, *guḍūcī*, *rāsnā*, *aśvagandhā*, *amaradāru*, *pāṭhā*, *tvak*, the two types of *bala*, *tagara*, sesame seeds, *mūrvā*, horse-gram (*kulattha*), *nalada*, and *ghana* (musta); 69. *Punarnavā*, the bark of bamboo fruit, *jīvantī*, cardamom (*elā*), *aguru*, *jīvaka*, the root of *eraṇḍa*, the shoots of good fruit, and the flowers of *kuraṇḍa*.

And [the use of] the five great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadha). // 69 // Boiled with two or three of these in water, or with goat’s milk, cow’s milk, or even sheep’s milk, along with a little rock salt (saindhava), this liquid, when slightly warm, serves as a soothing eye-drop (āścyotana) for eye diseases caused by Vāta. // 70 // Dārvī, utpala, padmaka, tugayāṣā, medā, mṛṇāla, madhuka, samaṅgā, kālīyaka, parpaṭaka, latā, and drākṣā; then kārṣmarya and parūṣaka; // 71 // The roots of gundrā, naḍa, and vetasa, and the flowerless buds of grasses;

Prapauṇḍarīka, kirātatikta, bhadraśrī, nimba, paṭola, and vāśā—[these] should be boiled in goat’s milk or in the milk of a woman; this [milk] used as an eye-drop (āścyotana) would be excellent for eye diseases caused by pitta and those characterized by blood. The three pungents (trikaṭu), triphalā, haridrā, kāsīsa, jātī, gṛhadhūma, jāti, lac (lākṣā), dantī, surasa, vacā, pāṭhā, aśvagandhā, and agrya amaradāru, along with kaṭphala, elā, aguru, and kaṇṭakārī—[this is the best formulation].

Rodhra, karañja, bṛhatī, and śvadaṃṣṭrā—two or three of these, along with rock salt, should be placed in water and made lukewarm. For eye diseases caused by phlegm (śleṣman), the wise prescribe an eye-drop (āścyotana) consisting of parūṣaka, āmrātaka, tintiḍīka, vṛkṣāmla, jambu, āmra, kapittha, and kola, mixed with a large quantity of honey.

Alternatively, an eye-drop (āścyotana) prepared with ten *mātuluṅga* fruits, or sour pomegranates, or fermented liquors (*madya*), or milk, or curd-whey (*dadhimastu*), or decoctions of *dārvī*, *utpala*, and other such herbs combined with sour substances and mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*), [should be used]. // 77 //

This [ointment] forcibly destroys eye diseases caused by blood (*raktātmikā*), whether produced by cold or heat, as well as those arising from a combination of humors or from all [humors] together, after carefully considering the deficiency or excess in the disease. The wise physician should apply this [treatment] which removes [the disease]. Eranda root, along with its fruits and sprouts, boiled in goat’s milk, is said by excellent physicians to be the foremost eye-drop (*āścyotana*) for removing *vātarakta*. Prapauṇḍarīka, Madhuka, and Haridrā... [and other ingredients]. (Verse 80)

An eye-drop (*āścyotana*) mixed with sugar will alleviate pain caused by *pitta* and *vāta*. A decoction of *nata*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *bṛhatī*, bark, and *hrīvera*, boiled in goat’s milk and water and combined with rock salt (*saindhava*), shall remove disorders of *vāta* and *kapha*. (81) An eye-drop [prepared thus] shall be a destroyer of wind and phlegm.

82–83. Madhuka and dārvī should be boiled in cow’s milk, or by a woman [in goat’s milk]; this eye-drop (āścyotana), mixed with sugar, should be administered by a skilled physician in cases of wind-blood (mārutaraktapitta). Having tied the fine powders of the fruit-exudate (phalatrava) upon a portion of a white linen cloth, [they should be placed] in goat’s milk by the woman.

Or, when immersed in water, it shall remove all diseases. *Dārvī*, *haridrā*, *triphalā*, and *musta*, combined with sugar and honey (verse 84), used as eye-drops (*āścyotana*) mixed with human milk, are declared the foremost remedy for destroying [disorders of] bile, blood, and wind. [Also effective are drops made from] fresh roots of the castor plant (*eraṇḍa*).

Then, with the pastes of the leaves along with sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika-taṇḍula*), one should prepare *śāvaraka* smeared with clarified butter according to the previous procedure; this will alleviate pain. (85–86) The physician should employ fomentation (*sveda*), poultice (*puṭapāka*), bandaging (*nāvana*), saturation (*tarpaṇa*), drinking of clarified butter, ointment (*lepa*), and affusion (*pariṣeka*) using these very substances prescribed for eye-drops (*āścyotana*). (87) They prescribe facial ointments (*mukhalepa*) that are beneficial according to the season and the disease, which remove discoloration (*abhīlu*, *vyaṅga*, *nīlikā*), as well as those that eliminate poison and swelling. (88) [These include] the bark of milky trees, sandalwood (*candana*), *padmaka*, *gundrā*, and lotus-root fiber (*mṛṇāla*).

7. And *ghanabālaka*, the roots of *kuśa*, *tagara*, *elavālu*, *tālīsapatra*, *nalada*, and sesame seeds; 89. *masūra*, *dūrvā*, *māyava*, lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*), and the juice of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and blue lotuses (*utpala*); *śaileya*, *mustā*, *aguru*, 8. *jhāmaka*, *sthauṇeyaka*, *elā*, *tagara*, and sesame seeds; 90. *tvak*, *patra*, *kuṣṭha*, *aguru*, *jhāmaka*, *māṃsī*, *hareṇu*, and *paripelava*; *yaṣṭi*, *hvara*, *rodhra*, *aguru*, *candana*, *punarnavā*, black sesame, and *latā*. Thus [these are] in pairs.

9. To be applied at the proper times, such as during the heat and so forth, by means of facial pastes; I have shown what is beneficial for the vision of men—now hear from me as I speak of those things that remove the humors (*doṣa*). 10. Those prescribed for the onset of the rainy season destroy wind-disorders (*vātāmaya*); those prescribed in autumn destroy bile-disorders (*pittāmaya*); those taught for the summer destroy blood-disorders; and those taught for the arrival of spring destroy phlegm-disorders (*kaphāmaya*). [The ingredients are: cotton roots, *uśīra*, *kālīyaka*, creepers, the bark of milky trees, and *bhadraśrī*.

11. They say that *kaṅgu* and barley are to be described as facial ointments (*vadanapralepa*). These, having been dried with cow urine, may be mixed with the juice of *kola* and *amlamūtra*, or they may be combined with mustard seeds and dried in the juice of *mātuluṅga*.
(Bower Manuscript, Folio 5)

95. [These] should be applied to the face when it is afflicted by impurities, when blood has been emitted, after the administration of oleation (sneha) or various purgatives (vireka), and when nasal therapy (nasya) has been performed. 96–97. A paste for the face (mukhapralepa) consisting of cinnamon bark (tvak), cardamom (patra), spikenard (māṃsī), tagara (nata), sandalwood (candana), realgar (manaḥśilā), tiger-claw (vyāghranakha), hareṇu, *x*, souryaka, kuṣṭha, surasa, and the two types of turmeric (haridrā) removes poison. A paste for the face made of mūrvā, aśvagandhā, triphalā, and karañja removes swelling. They say that mūrvā, when boiled in cow’s urine, also removes swelling.

3. It may serve as a facial ointment. (98) When the face is smeared with it, a person should not laugh, nor should he weep; likewise, he should not indulge in sleep, nor should he eat. He should not warm it over a fire, nor should he hold a dry ointment in his mouth. (99) The fearlessness, the blueness, as well as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), disfigurements, pustules, and moles of a living being are instantly pacified by this facial ointment; furthermore, both the vision and the countenance become clear. (100) When the face is smeared, while laughing or eating, phlegm together with wind [is expelled].

5. An irritation arising while one is sleeping quickly passes away from that head; therefore, purgatives, oleaginous substances, and medicinal smokes (dhūma) should be administered again. 101. When a person’s [medicinal paste] has melted due to the heat of fire, and it remains on the face after it has dried, they declare that diseases preceded by a burning sensation (abhīlu) will arise; for these, one should perform the pacification as previously described. 102. Night-blindness, timira, headache, burning, and eye-ache of a pitta-nature accompanied by burning—as well as other disorders located in the mouth and skin—are immediately pacified.

7. From the application of ointments to the face: // 103 // They declare that facial ointments are to be avoided in cases of disorders of the eyes caused by phlegm or wind, for those who have undergone nasal therapy (*nastaḥkarma*), for those suffering from chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*), and likewise in cases of lockjaw (*hanugraha*) and headaches. A quarter of a finger-breadth [is the measure]. // 104 //

The application of a facial paste (mukhalepa) is prescribed: the middling [dose] should be three parts, while the lowest should be half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula). [The ingredients are: yaṣṭī, hvarodhra, triphalā, mṛṇāla, white sugar (sitopalā), and kāñcanagairika; as well as patra, tvak, elā, aguru, devadāru, punarnavā, vyāghranakha, and añjana. 105–106.

9–10. Realgar, *bṛhatī* bark, *māṃsī*, *hareṇu*, *paripelava*, *sauvīraka*, red ochre, *kaṭphala*, and *śārivā* mixed with sugar—these four formulations, each consisting of half [the quantity of sugar], are prescribed for the pacification of diseases caused by *kapha*, blood, *pitta*, and *anila*. With these *viḍālaka* applications, one should rub the eye all around, starting from the root of the eyelashes, or apply them externally. Alternatively, a *viḍālaka* consists of *rodhra* slightly smeared with ghee, or *abhayā* rubbed on iron, or the bark of *bṛhatī* combined with an equal amount of collyrium (*añjana*).

11. It shall be a remover of all diseases. // 109 // Equal parts of red ochre (*gairika*), *rasāñjana*, *añjana*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and *rītikusuma*, with a small amount of black pepper added, [and] twice as much *x x x x x x x x*... // 110 //

One should cook marica and kusuma with ghee over a gentle fire. This is the *añjanaviḍālaka* [ointment]; we shall now describe its fourfold application. ... [regarding] baldness and graying hair in the cow... listen as it is being proclaimed: Due to the corruption of the bodily fluids (*rasa*), from excessive sexual indulgence, and from the vitiation of bile and blood, premature graying occurs; in the elderly, it arises through the process of aging. Generally, women are of phlegmatic constitution (*śleṣmala*), and their shadow is like a thorn... [the rest of the verse is fragmentary].

Those who indulge in [such things] produce the corrupted *rajas*. Therefore, the hair-bearing ground of women possesses clear blood, bile, and heat; consequently, their hairs do not fall out, and for that reason, women do not become bald. Because of this, in men, when there is a reversal [of these conditions], the blood and bile become vitiated. [The menstrual period occurs] during the *ṛtu*.

The roots of the hair indeed cause baldness of the head. Baldness that is hairless, copper-colored at the roots, and long-standing is not curable; however, that which is recent should be properly treated. In cases of baldness and premature graying, one should first repeatedly perform venesection.

For one whose vitiated blood has been purified, emesis and other such procedures are beneficial. Once the digestive tract is thus cleansed, as previously described, one should subsequently employ various oil formulations as well as hair-dyes; likewise, those that generate hair and those that cause it to grow.

6. And washing the hair is beneficial for removing defects. {O} The wise physician should treat one suffering from cough caused by *vāta* with ghees prepared with sweet, sour, and salty ingredients, along with rice, or with them alone, according to the patient's strength. [He should also treat him] with the juices of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, together with jaggery and onions.

(253) A dose of one *karṣa* should be administered for abdominal tumors (*jaṭharī*) and gulmas; likewise, a wise physician should employ it for those suffering from *kacchapa* disease. (254) One should drink warm water after it, because of the small quantity of this clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). This [medicine], by a single application, breaks up gulmas—whether they are accumulated, painful, or accompanied by constriction—just as the wind disperses the clouds. Indeed, this clarified butter has been prepared for the purpose of destroying the five types of gulmas. (255–256)

"Just as the self-existent one [created] the thunderbolt for the sake of slaying all the Asuras, so this 'Drop-Ghee' (Bindughṛta) has been proclaimed—perfected and esteemed by the perfected ones. (257) [The *Āśvinabindughṛta*: Goat's milk, ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), *vacā*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), myrobalan (*harītakī*), long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marica*), *pāṭhā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and ghee as the tenth ingredient. (258) The portions of the ingredients beginning with ginger and ending with the salt should each be one *palika*. One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with four times as much goat's milk. (259) Through its use, one shall obtain memory and intelligence.

9. For a human being, the state of being dull-witted, stammering, or mute is pacified simply by drinking this [mixture]. [End of Chapter Two] I shall now describe *balā-taila*, which destroys diseases of the wind (*vāta*), is approved by Ātreya, is proven effective, brings about conception for barren women, and is auspicious. (261)

One hundred palas of dried roots of *balā*, twenty-five palas of *guḍūcī*, and ten palas of *rāsnā* should be taken. Having washed and crushed them, one should boil them in one hundred *āḍhakas* of divine water until one *āḍhaka* remains. With that excellent decoction, one should cook one *āḍhaka* of oil, along with curd-whey (*dadhimastu*), fermented gruel (*śukta*), and likewise sugarcane juice. // 262–264 //

One should slowly cook half a portion of goat’s milk over a mild fire, and add these following ingredients, each weighing one *pala*, which are to be ground into a paste: the roots of *balā* and *atibalā*, *sarala*, *devadāru*, *musta*, *madhuka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *tagara*, *padmaka*, *aguru*, *hareṇu*, *elā*, and *vyāghranakha*.

One should know that when the *kesara*, *surasa*, *ṣaḍī*, *mudgaparṇī*, *māṣaparṇī*, and both *jīvaka* and *ṛṣabhaka* have been prepared, one should then remove it from the fire; and once removed, the physician should administer the paste of the leaves.

Having strained that [decoction] while it is clear, one should place it in a clean vessel; then the wise physician should administer it according to the disease and according to the patient's strength. This should be employed for massage, nasal administration (nastaḥpāna), oil enemas (anuvāsana), in food, and likewise for the ears, as well as for enemas and urethral/vaginal enemas (uttaravasti).

Whether it be wasting away, or cough, or dyspnea, or fever; or fainting, or vomiting, or debility, or discoloration of the complexion; swelling, disorders of the semen, or even abdominal tumors (gulma) or splenic enlargement; hernias, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), consumption, or heat and pain in the head. (271–272)

This oil cures epilepsy (apasmāra) and "the bow-stiffness" (dhanuṣkaṃbha); it pacifies all those Vātas that have reached the skin, those that have resorted to the marrow, those that have entered the vessels (sirā), those that have reached the tendons (snāyu), and those that are systemic—of this there is no doubt. One should administer it to women during their fertile period after they have bathed their heads; by practicing this application, even a barren woman conceives. The physician should give this auspicious Bala-oil, which pacifies discoloration of the complexion and subdues misfortune (alakṣmī).

"The Increase of the Strength of the Faculties" (Balendriyavivardhana), verse 276. {X} *Bala*-oil, verse 16: {X} One should cook half an *āḍhaka* of oil with a decoction of one hundred *bala* plants, using the pastes (*kalka*) of *madhuka*, *māñjiṣṭhā*, *candana*, *utpala*, and *padmaka*; together with fragrant substances, the *jīvanīya* group, and two *droṇas* of milk. Verse 277.

This *balā-taila* is worthy of kings; it removes disorders of wind (*vāta*). By this same method, one should cook oils named after *rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, and *madhuka*, as well as that of *sahacara*. [Regarding *balā-taila*: A wise man should take one hundred well-measured palas of *balā* root and boil it in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth. One should cook that milk with a gentle fire; by this procedure, one should decoct the oil ten times. This prepared Bala-oil destroys many diseases; it is prescribed for drinking, massage, food, nasal administration, and enemas.

In all seasonal diseases, those based on *rakta-pitta*, in cases of morbid uterine conditions, and in men whose semen has been lost; in cases of dryness of the palate, thirst, burning sensations, pain in the flanks, abnormal menstrual flow, wasting, consumption, insanity, and erysipelas (visarpa). (284–285)

(text continues) ... this indeed is the highest [remedy].

This oil increases nourishment (287); it pacifies all diseases, is worthy of kings, and is like nectar. This oil, renowned by the name Amṛta, bestows strength upon men (288). crystal, silver, gold, gems, and pearl-oysters (300). [And] yaṣṭīmadhuka, māñjiṣṭhā, and aṃśumatī—one pala each of these—having ground them finely, one should cook them slowly over a gentle fire (301) with four bowl-measures of oil. From that oil...

Indeed, by the application of this nectar, women conceive; it cures all eighty diseases born of wind (vāta), blood (rakta), bile (pitta), phlegm (śleṣman), and those arising from the combination of the humors (sannipāta). This [oil] removes evil, destroys misfortune, and increases prosperity. "And [this] should be given to women who desire offspring. (324) {X} Root-Radish Oil {X} One *prastha* of root-radish juice and one *prastha* of milk should be prepared. Once that has turned into curd, it should be combined with one *prastha* of oil. [Add] *yaṣṭīmadhuka*... (325)

2. Rāsnā, pāṭhā, jaggery, and ginger—one *ardhapala* (half-pala) of each of these should be ground with water. 326. There should be one *karṣa* of salt; this should be cooked slowly over a mild fire. One should boil four hundred palas of *sahacara*, finely ground, in four *droṇas* of water. When reduced to one *droṇa* and strained, one should slowly cook one *āḍhaka* of oil with ten palas of the paste of the roots of *sahacara*. (329–330)

Having strained it and made it pleasantly warm, one should add ten and eight *palas* of sugar to it; then, having stirred it well, one should set it aside. It is highly recommended for enemas, internal drinking, massage, and nasal administration. It is effective for hemiplegia, facial paralysis, lockjaw, and headaches.

This oil pacifies facial paralysis (*ardita*), trembling, insanity, fever with stiffness of all limbs, sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*), wind-tumors (*vātagulma*), and those whose minds are afflicted by spirits; it also cures epilepsy (*apasmāra*), the "bow-bending" (*dhanuṣkambha*), stiffness of the thighs (*ūrūṣkambha*), *alāsaka*, swellings of the cheeks, ears, and scrotum, as well as the contraction of the hands and knees. It likewise subdues the loosening of joints and bones, trembling, and wasting away—just as the wind disperses the clouds after cutting through them. [This applies] even in the absence of sugar.

One should cook it with milk; this was established by the Self-Existent One for the purpose of destroying the host of diseases. (336) Regarding *sahacara-taila*: one should cook a *prastha* of oil from dehusked sesame seeds, adding one *pala* of *madhuka* and four times as much milk. (337) When that has been cooked gently, one should cook it again; according to this procedure, one should properly cook a hundred measures of *madhuka*. (338) It should be cooked a hundred times, and one should set aside this "hundred-cooked" (*śatapāka*) [oil] for both drinking and as an ointment. (338)

It is not recommended for consumption during the rainy season or autumn. For men suffering from *rājayakṣman* (consumption), it is like nectar when taken as food. It subdues heart disease, dryness of the palate, *pittagulma*, *pratānaka* (epilepsy), thirst, insanity, erysipelas, asthma, cough, and malignant jaundice.

It also checks excessive hemorrhaging, upward-moving blood (*sarvatobhāga-ūrdhvaga*), jaundice, fever, and anemia. Furthermore, it cures the suppuration of *pitta*, burning sensations, eruptive boils, and scabies.

Whatever various diseases afflict brahmins are pacified by this oil, just as dust is settled at the arrival of the rains. [This is] the oil named Madhuyaṣṭika. Having boiled one hundred palas of the roots of *hayagandhā* in a vessel... [it should be] prepared in four [measures] of water until one-fourth remains, and then strained. [The ingredients are: *madhuka*, ginger, *suradāru*, *śatāvarī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *analada*, *kuṣṭha*, the two types of *karañja*, *savarṣabhū*, lotus stalk (*amṛṇāla*), *śatapuṣpā*, *surasa*, *rāsnā*, and *payasyā*.

And three [palas] each of ṣaḍī, puṣkaramūla, sthirā, dravantī, and payasyā (346)—having thoroughly ground all these ingredients into a paste weighing one karṣa each and stirred them into a decoction, one should cook one āḍhaka of oil over a mild fire, adding four times as much milk (347). It should be stored in a clean place; it is to be used for drinking, as an ointment, for enemas, and in the process of medicinal infusion. Those whose vital seed is exhausted, those who are impotent from envy, and those afflicted by lockjaw—[for them] there is horse-radish oil. Half a *tulā* of the roots of the horse-radish (*aśvagandhā*), cut into pieces, should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water until it is reduced to one-eighth.

Listen as I declare the diseases for which this should be administered: for men who are lame or mute, those afflicted by thigh-stiffness (*ūrūṣkambha*), those with hemiplegia (*pakṣahīna*), those with fractures, and those whose bones and joints have been displaced; this is for those with Vāta-induced injuries.

And when the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) have perished; in cases of lockjaw (*hanugraha*), facial paralysis (*khaḍa*), and urinary disorders (*meha*); those who have been cast down by *vāta*; in those afflicted by *vāta*-fractures and the dejected; likewise in those whose sense faculties are diminished; and those men whose semen has vanished, as well as those who are envious or impotent (*īrṣyā-śaṇḍha*). The third chapter, on the preparation of oils, within the *Siddhasaṃkarṣa* section of the *Nāvanītaka*, is concluded. Hereafter, we shall describe miscellaneous formulations. Seven *pippalī* fruits, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *kuṣṭha*, combined with cow’s urine, constitute a purgative. Jaggery, grape juice, honey, and likewise *harītakī*—this is the purgative for those with a predominance of bile (*paittika*) proclaimed by Kāṅkāyana. (934–935)

And it quickly brings [the disease] under control. Fol. 29: Bower Manuscript, r1 Through the application of *harītakī*, swelling (*śvayathu*) is split open; [it expels] dysentery (*pravāhikā*) along with water, as if by the wind (*maruta*) itself. (943) It likewise destroys diseases such as phlegm-bile, blood-bile, jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*), and chlorosis (*halīmaka*), as well as those [caused by] *abhaya*... (944) This *harītakī* indeed destroys excessive salivation due to phlegm, discoloration, hoarseness of voice, loss of appetite, heart disease, and fainting. (945) Just as the powerful Vaiśvānara fire becomes [all the more] potent when joined with the wind, so too does it become endowed with its full potency.

Harītakī may be taken with jaggery (guḍa). Regarding this, there is a verse: In whatever manner it may be—whether drunk mixed with jaggery, administered by a physician, or licked—it renders the diseases of men, even those that are difficult to overcome and long-standing, into non-diseases. There is no disease among humans on earth that this Harītakī would not forcibly conquer. Therefore, a wise person should employ that illustrious fruit, born of nectar, in every respect. Salt is beneficial for horses; water is praised for elephants; and fire is [beneficial] for cows.

"The lotus-born [Brahmā] has declared that *harītakī* is the most excellent for the medical treatment of men. Thus ends the *Harītakī-kalpa*, belonging to the month of Āśvina. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *Śilājatu-kalpa*. Śilājatu is neither too hot nor too astringent; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*). One should understand its origin from four minerals: gold, silver, copper, and black iron. When processed according to the prescribed methods, it is an elixir (*rasāyana*) and an aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*).

And that [substance] is a destroyer of disease (7). When well-impregnated with decoctions (*niryūha*) that subdue wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*), it attains a supreme excellence of potency, whether by all [the decoctions] together or even one by one (952). Having first prepared the receptacle by adding and stirring [the impregnating liquid], one should then pour that [substance] into the liquid; for seven days it should be kept in this manner, according to this procedure, for its impregnation (953). Together with the powders of the metals mentioned previously, when drunk with milk, it bestows long life accompanied by happiness (954). It pacifies aging and secondary diseases and brings firmness to the body.

9. It produces intelligence and memory, and is strengthening; one who subsists on milk should employ it. 955. Its administration is for seven weeks, three days, and one week; thus its application is prescribed as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. 956. The dosage is one *pala*, half a *pala*, or the smallest dose being half a *karṣa*. Hereafter I shall describe its specific varieties along with the procedure. 957. When minerals from the mountains, such as gold and others, heated by the sun, exude a substance that is glossy, heavy, earthy, and clear, that is *śilājatu*. 958.

That which is sweet and slightly bitter, resembling the *japā* flower in color, and pungent and cold in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), is the exudation of gold. That which is copper-colored, resembling the throat of a peacock, sharp and hot, and pungent when digested, is that of silver. That which is white, pungent, cold, and sweet in its post-digestive effect is that of silver.

It is bitter and cold in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and that which is of iron origin is the best of all. It has the smell of cow’s urine; all [types] are suitable for every medical application, but the last one is distinguished for the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*). They specifically praise [these] impurities, such as *hemamala* and others, for wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), and especially for bile and phlegm in the three [doshas]. In the administration of *śilājatu*, one should always avoid heavy foods that cause indigestion, and one must strictly avoid horse-gram (*kulattha*).

Milk products, fermented liquids, juices along with soured gruels, water mixed with urine, and various decoctions—having carefully examined those specific regions where these were perfected for the purpose of stirring *śilājatu*, they should be employed. There is no disease on earth that can be cured which *śilājatu* does not forcibly conquer; therefore, when applied through various methods of administration, it bestows manifold vigor upon the healthy person. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparation (*kalpa*) of *citraka*. [To] the greatly wise Dhānvantari...

Keśava asked: "Is there any medicinal herb at all that can thus eliminate every disease? Having heard Keśava's words, Dhanvantari replied: "In this world, it is said that there is no medicine equal to the *citraka*."

That [medicine] should be known to be of three kinds: black, white, and yellow. One should designate their quality as superior, inferior, or middling according to this sequence. One should know that the black variety is beneficial for those with skin diseases, urinary disorders (prameha), and likewise for those with abdominal dropsy; it is especially so for those afflicted with leucoderma (śvitrin). The white-flowered variety is designated as a destroyer of disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids, a cure for diarrhea, a stabilizer of youth, and a promoter of intelligence. The yellow variety generates intelligence, vital energy, and digestive fire, and it subdues phlegm (kapha).

It is traditionally taught that one should prescribe [the medicines] which destroy wind, bile, and phlegm in their proper sequence. Having gathered all of them according to what is available, one should employ them. One should extract [the roots] either in the month of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, or Āṣāḍha. Specifically, one should extract the black variety in Kārttika, the white in Mārgaśīrṣa, or the yellow in Āṣāḍha; such is the proper time for its collection. Having worshipped the gods according to the rules and having had the Brahmins recite auspicious blessings, one should [collect it] in a place avoided by cremation grounds, saline soil, anthills, and sacred shrines.

This treatment, cooling as snow, should be employed for one in whose body eruptions (*visphoṭaka*) and a burning sensation (*paridāha*) are observed. One should treat such a person with bitter, sweet, and cold decoctions (*kaṣāya*). Now, a powder of *parpaṭaka*, *uśīra*, and white clay—having taken all these in equal parts—one should apply a beneficial ointment made from them ground together. One should also prepare an ointment consisting of *saugandhika*, sugar, the filaments of the *kumuda* lotus, sandalwood, and *mañjiṣṭhā*.

For a child, one should apply a plaster made of sugar, oyster shell, pearl-oyster, conch-shell, young grass, and cane; this destroys eruptive boils (*visphoṭaka*). In cases of mouth-sores (*mukhapāka*), one should apply a plaster of grapes mixed with honey. Furthermore, one should cleanse the child’s mouth with *rasāñjana* and honey. Indeed, for the child who, due to mouth-sores, refuses the mother’s breast, one should treat him with the tender shoots of the *sumanā* jasmine mixed with honey.

One should rub [the area] with an arrow-shaft splinter and ink; one should perform this rubbing with this paste. Having recognized that the mouth is purified, one should rub it with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*). Then, having ground together *dhātakī*, *sallakī*, *jiṅgaṇī*, *samaṅgā*, and *rohiṇī*, one should cook oil. For ear discharge (*karṇasrāva*), after repeatedly cleansing the ear with ear-oil, [one should apply] that which is prepared with *bilva* and sandalwood.

And oil should be used for filling [the ear] as it is beneficial; likewise, a paste of *bilva* cooked with the juice of *kapittha* [is recommended]. Milk should be applied to the ear, as is oil that cleanses the channels (*srotas*). Oil cooked with all the fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*) is praised for putrid ears (*pūtikarṇa*). Once the ear has been purified, fumigation should be performed with *akṣa* and *guggulu*. When the ears are afflicted by pain, a wise person should fill them with scented oil (*gandhataila*), and also with the juice of radish (*mūlaka*).
